claims.text: What the strip looks like A narrow-complex, regular tachycardia, typically 150–250, with P waves often buried in the QRS or seen as a retrograde pseudo-R' in V1.
claims.quote: Narrow complex, regular, rate typically 150–250 P waves often buried in QRS or appear as retrograde pseudo-R' in V1

claims.text: Aspects (abnormal in red) Rate and rhythm: regular tachycardia, about 140–280
QRS: narrow (< 120 ms) unless a co-existing bundle branch block, accessory pathway or rate-related aberrancy
claims.quote: Narrow QRS complexes (< 120ms) unless there is co-existing bundle branch block, accessory pathway, or rate-related aberrant conduction

claims.text: P waves: retrograde (inverted in II, III, aVF) if seen — buried in the QRS, just after it, or very rarely before it
claims.quote: P waves if visible exhibit retrograde conduction with P-wave inversion in leads II, III, aVF. They may be buried within, visible after, or very rarely visible before the QRS complex

claims.text: Typical (slow-fast) AVNRT: P waves often hidden in the QRS; pseudo-R' in V1 or V2; pseudo-S in II, III or aVF
claims.quote: P waves are often hidden – being embedded in the QRS complexes Pseudo R’ wave may be seen in V1 or V2 Pseudo S waves may be seen in leads II, III or aVF

claims.text: Associated: rate-related ST depression (with or without coronary disease); QRS alternans (beat-to-beat amplitude variation with normal voltage)
claims.quote: Rate-related ST depression, which may be seen with or without underlying coronary artery disease QRS alternans – phasic variation in QRS amplitude associated with AVNRT and AVRT, distinguished from electrical alternans by a normal QRS amplitude

claims.text: Onset: abrupt onset and offset (paroxysmal) — typical of re-entry involving the AV node (AVNRT, AVRT)
claims.quote: Paroxysmal SVT (pSVT) describes an SVT with abrupt onset and offset – characteristically seen with re-entrant tachycardias involving the AV node such as AVNRT or atrioventricular re-entry tachycardia (AVRT)

claims.text: Causes (mechanism and diagnoses) Mechanism: a functional re-entry circuit within the AV node (AVRT instead uses an anatomical accessory pathway)
claims.quote: In comparison to AVRT, which involves an anatomical re-entry circuit (Bundle of Kent), in AVNRT there is a functional re-entry circuit within the AV node.

claims.text: Slow-fast circuit: a PAC finds the fast pathway still refractory, goes down the slow pathway, returns up the fast pathway, and keeps cycling around the two
claims.quote: 1) A premature atrial contraction (PAC) arrives while the fast pathway is still refractory, and is directed down the slow pathway 2) The ERP in the fast pathway ends, and the PAC impulse travels retrogradely up the fast pathway 3) The impulse continually cycles around the two pathways

claims.text: Triggers: spontaneous, or exertion, caffeine, alcohol, beta-agonists (salbutamol), sympathomimetics (amphetamines)
claims.quote: AVNRT is typically paroxysmal and may occur spontaneously or upon provocation with exertion, caffeine, alcohol, beta-agonists (salbutamol) or sympathomimetics (amphetamines)

claims.text: The commonest cause of palpitations in structurally normal hearts
claims.quote: This is the commonest cause of palpitations in patients with structurally normal hearts

claims.text: Symptoms Sudden onset of rapid, regular palpitations; also presyncope or syncope, chest pain, dyspnea, anxiety, and rarely polyuria
claims.quote: Patients will typically complain of the sudden onset of rapid, regular palpitations. Other associated symptoms may include: Presyncope or syncope due to a transient fall in blood pressure Chest pain, especially in the context of underlying coronary artery disease Dyspnoea Anxiety Rarely, polyuria due to elevated atrial pressures causing release of atrial natriuretic peptide

claims.text: Attacks last a few seconds to several hours (rarely > 12 hours)
claims.quote: Attacks may last only a few seconds or persist for several hours (rarely, > 12 hours).

claims.text: Vagal maneuvers: Valsalva, unilateral carotid sinus massage, ice-water facial immersion, swallowing ice-cold water — may terminate it, particularly if used early
claims.quote: Vagotonic maneuvers (eg, Valsalva maneuver, unilateral carotid sinus massage, ice water facial immersion, swallowing of ice-cold water), particularly if used early, may terminate the tachyarrhythmia

claims.text: Adenosine (first-choice drug): 6 mg rapid IV bolus, then a 20-mL saline bolus; if ineffective, two 12-mg doses every 5 minutes
claims.quote: Adenosine is the first choice. Dose is 6 mg by rapid IV bolus (0.05 to 0.1 mg/kg in children), followed by a 20-mL saline bolus. If this dosage is ineffective, 2 subsequent 12-mg doses are given every 5 minutes.

claims.text: If adenosine is ineffective: verapamil or diltiazem
claims.quote: Use atrioventricular (AV) nodal blockers for narrow complex tachycardia; adenosine is the first choice, and if ineffective, verapamil or diltiazem are alternatives.

claims.text: Frequent or bothersome episodes: catheter ablation is preferred and usually curative
claims.quote: When episodes of reentrant (paroxysmal) supraventricular tachycardia are frequent or bothersome, transvenous catheter ablation is the preferred treatment and is usually curative
